claims.text: The target material is HfNbTaTiZr containing up to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
This oxygen-containing material has realistic defect and disorder levels.
Lattice and electronic heat transport can be computed separately by explicitly modeling atomic-scale disorder, defect scattering, and anharmonic phonon interactions.
The proposed model is applicable from approximately 200 K to 1200 K.
Both lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions are significant yet distinguishable within the proposed 200–1200 K range.
Oxygen impurity atoms induce defect scattering and anharmonic phonon interactions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Atomic-mass variation, defect density, and anharmonicity mediate heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Combining DFT-derived elastic properties with temperature-dependent phonon-scattering models captures defect scattering and anharmonicity.
Separating lattice and electronic calculations avoids oversimplifications associated with perfect-crystal or Debye-based assumptions.
The proposed framework will outperform earlier approaches.
The model will predict total thermal conductivity within ±10–15% of experimental values.
The model will accurately resolve separate lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions.
Total thermal conductivity is expected to be approximately 10–17 W/(K m).
Lattice and electronic contributions are expected to be comparable at lower temperatures.
Existing models use perfect-crystal assumptions or simplified Debye-temperature or phenomenological treatments.
Existing models often conflate lattice and electronic heat transport and have larger deviations from experiment.
The approach is limited to nominally single-phase HfNbTaTiZr with no more than roughly 1 wt.% oxygen.
The model may not be valid for samples with secondary phases or substantially different defect concentrations.
Wiedemann–Franz analysis can provide an independent high-temperature assessment of the electronic thermal-conductivity contribution.
Failure to predict total conductivity within ±10–15%, or failure to reproduce measured lattice/electronic partitioning, would falsify the hypothesis.
